title: Landmark Deal Would Officially Add Laser Weapons to US Army Arsenal
gist: The US Army is poised to sign a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars with AeroVironment for up to 20 Enduring High Energy Laser (E-HEL) systems to defend bases against drones — the first time a laser weapon becomes an Army 'program of record' inscribed in the Pentagon's five-year budget after 50 years of failed attempts. The economic driver is cost-per-shot asymmetry ($4 million Patriot interceptors fired at $35,000 Iranian drones) plus a March 1 attack that killed six US service members; the author, who wrote a 2006 cover story predicting lasers would end the era of bombs and bullets, argues lasers remain a complement to guns and missiles, not a replacement, because rain, fog and one-target-at-a-time engagement still cap them.

themes.theme: Program of record as the real signal

insights.claim: The materially novel element of the AeroVironment deal is not the hardware but the designation: E-HEL becomes an operational 'program of record' formally inscribed in the Pentagon's five-year budget, the first time the Army has ever done so for a laser weapon.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Program-of-record status converts episodic prototype dollars into a budgeted multi-year revenue line — the distinction that separates a press-release contract from a durable earnings stream for a defense supplier.

insights.claim: Program-of-record designation functions as an institutional signal in two directions: internal validation that the capability is real, and an instruction to contractors to ramp production capacity.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
entities: Rapid Capabilities and Critical Technologies Office
insights.so_what: Watch program-of-record announcements as the trigger for supplier capex and hiring in directed energy — the supply chain moves on the designation, not the first delivery order.
insights.quote: Program of record indicates a wider cultural acceptance of the new technology as a military capability,
insights.locator: That's the military's sign to itself

insights.claim: The expected contract covers up to 20 weapons per the Army's original request for information, with each system compact enough to fit in a four-by-seven foot container or mount atop an all-terrain vehicle.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Initial unit volumes are small — this is an option on a follow-on production ramp, not a revenue event; size positions against the 20-unit base case, not the total addressable base count.
insights.locator: Now, the Army is expected to sign a contract

insights.claim: The economic case for directed energy is a two-order-of-magnitude interceptor mismatch: during the early Iran conflict the US fired $4 million Patriot missiles at $35,000 Iranian drones, wasting money and depleting the American interceptor stockpile.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Munitions inventory depletion, not budget, is the binding constraint in drone-saturated theaters — the strongest structural argument for directed energy and for interceptor restocking programs simultaneously.
insights.locator: The Iran and Ukraine wars have shown

insights.claim: Lasers' defining advantage is a magazine constrained only by power supply rather than by rounds, making them the natural counter to saturation drone swarms — though refire and recharge rates remain unsolved engineering problems.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Power generation and thermal management, not optics, are the gating technologies for laser weapon value — that is where the supplier moat and the capex will sit.
insights.quote: Basically, you can keep firing them as long as you've got power,
insights.locator: Modern lasers, on the other hand, never run out of ammunition

insights.claim: The forcing event was lethal, not budgetary: on March 1 an Iranian drone killed six US service members and injured 30, after jammers, microwave weapons, missiles and counter-drones had each proven insufficient in isolation.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Casualty events, not capability demos, unlock Pentagon procurement speed — expect layered counter-UAS spending across multiple modalities rather than a single winning system.
insights.locator: The Pentagon and its suppliers had been scrambling

insights.claim: Top-level political endorsement frames lasers as a direct substitute for Patriot batteries at far lower cost, with the President publicly claiming lasers will soon do the work of Patriots.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Presidential framing of lasers as Patriot substitutes creates political tailwind for directed-energy budgets but also sets an expectations bar the physics section of this article says the technology cannot meet.
insights.quote: It’s coming out pretty soon, where literally lasers will do the work of—at a lot less cost—do the work of what the Patriots are doing.
insights.locator: Two days after the White Sands display

insights.claim: The technology converged on fiber lasers — bundles of glass wires infused with rare-earth ions — because they absorb energy more efficiently, shed heat better, and produce an almost perfectly focused beam, replacing toxic chemical lasers and weak crystal designs.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Rare-earth-doped fiber is the supply-chain chokepoint for weapons-grade lasers — a second-order exposure to rare-earth sourcing beyond magnets and EVs.
insights.locator: Eventually, most military laser-makers all turned

insights.claim: Individual fiber lasers produce only a few kilowatts and must be bundled for weapons-grade output, but small drones require relatively little power to destroy — meaning the target class, not the laser, defines feasibility.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Counter-drone lasers are viable today while counter-cruise-missile lasers are not; scale exposure to the low-power counter-UAS mission, not to the full missile-defense narrative.
insights.locator: Each individual fiber laser can't produce that much power

insights.claim: The unlock came from adjacent commercial technologies: semiconductor diode pumps, machine vision for target lock, and adaptive optics that flex mirrors in real time to cancel atmospheric shimmer.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Directed energy is a systems-integration play riding semiconductor and computer-vision cost curves, which favors integrators with commercial photonics supply over pure defense primes.
insights.locator: "Exciting" the atoms inside those fibers got easier

insights.claim: The Pentagon's own research leadership has publicly reclassified directed energy from a science problem to an engineering problem, with the implied consequence being cheaper, smaller and more proliferated systems.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: The 'engineering phase' framing is procurement language for volume buys — it precedes multi-year production contracts and unit-cost declines.
insights.quote: The science for directed energy is largely done, and now we are in the engineering phase of it. So the engineering part of it makes it cheaper, smaller, and more proliferated,
insights.locator: Emil Michael, the under secretary of defense

themes.theme: Hard physical limits and deployment failures

insights.claim: Lasers are defeated by rain and fog and must engage one target at a time for several seconds each, so a mass attack of roughly 1,000 drones cannot be fully intercepted by directed energy.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Directed energy will layer onto, not replace, kinetic interceptors — the counter-UAS budget expands rather than rotates, which is bullish for both categories.
insights.quote: So if you've got 1,000 drones coming in, you're not going to hit every single one,
insights.locator: Rain and fog stop lasers short

insights.claim: Field deployments have already produced real failures: four vehicles with Raytheon air-defense lasers were pulled from the Middle East after poor soldier reviews, and an AeroVironment laser on the southern US border zapped a party balloon in February, forcing the FAA to close El Paso airspace before the same system mistakenly shot down a Border Patrol drone.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Operator acceptance and airspace deconfliction are the near-term execution risks that could delay fielding even with budget secured — track soldier-feedback-driven withdrawals as the leading failure mode.
insights.locator: The deployments haven't all gone great

insights.claim: The accidental Border Patrol drone shootdown paradoxically strengthened the procurement case by demonstrating the weapon could actually destroy that class of target — a rare instance where a safety failure served as capability proof.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Watch for the same dynamic in other autonomy and weapons programs: incidents that would sink a commercial product can accelerate defense adoption when they prove lethality.
insights.quote: In fact, in some ways, the accidental kill helped make the case for the laser, proving it could actually take out such a drone.

insights.claim: High-power lasers do not attenuate at range the way munitions do — beams continue into orbit, creating collateral hazard to aircraft and satellites that has no analogue in kinetic air defense.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: An unpriced liability and likely future regulatory constraint on ground-based laser deployment near civil airspace and over satellite ground tracks.

insights.claim: The author explicitly discounts his own prior hype cycle, noting he wrote the 2006 Popular Science cover story asking whether lasers could end the era of bombs and bullets, and answering that the answer then and now is no.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Directed-energy narratives have a documented 20-year history of overpromising; discount capability claims and underwrite only the budgeted program-of-record cash flows.
insights.quote: I wrote that story. And the answer, then and now, is no.
insights.locator: It's a song we've heard before

insights.claim: The correct doctrinal framing is complementarity, not substitution: guns and missiles work, and lasers should be used for missions guns cannot perform rather than as a replacement for them.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Reject the substitution thesis in defense-budget models; laser adoption is additive spend concentrated in the cheap-target, high-volume defensive niche.
insights.quote: The gun works fine. Why would you replace it with the laser? Use the laser in ways that you can't use the gun.

insights.claim: The US military currently has roughly a half-dozen laser weapon systems deployed or in active testing, including Navy 'dazzlers' on two ships that blind drone electro-optical sensors and Boeing's Compact Laser Weapons System sent across the Air Force's Europe and Africa theater.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: The competitive field is already multi-vendor and multi-service; the AeroVironment award is a share-of-a-growing-pie event, not a monopoly grant.

insights.claim: Supplier-tier economics are already scaling independently: nLight, which supplies lasers to companies including AeroVironment, won its own Pentagon contract worth up to $627 million to develop a laser capable of destroying a cruise missile.
insights.speaker: Noah Shachtman
insights.so_what: Component suppliers may capture more directed-energy value than integrators, and the cruise-missile-class contract signals ambitions well beyond the counter-drone mission.
insights.locator: says Scott Keeney, the CEO of nLight
